content: Luxury spending is holding up in parts of Asia even as the AI-fueled stock-market rallies that helped create new wealth have stumbled. In South Korea and Japan, affluent consumers are still spending on jewelry, watches, and other luxury goods after huge gains in AI-linked stocks swelled household wealth. The trend is most apparent in South Korea, where Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and other technology companies powered a historic stock-market rally earlier this year. Markets have since turned volatile, but consumer spending has proved more resilient. "Buoyant revenues for technology firms have helped to drive large bonuses and dividend payouts, as well as wealth effects from rising stock prices, the combined impact of which has boosted consumption spending in the first half of 2026," Rajiv Biswas, CEO of Asia-Pacific Economics, told Business Insider. Korean spending slowed in July before rebounding in September, a dip the bank attributed partly to market swings, Kathleen Oh, the chief Korea and Taiwan economist at Morgan Stanley, wrote in a September 17 report. She added that consumer confidence in the spending recovery remained intact. The bank raised its forecast for private consumption growth this year to 2.6% from 2.2%, citing stronger household incomes, fiscal support, rising wealth, and inbound tourism. The resilience is showing up at department stores. At Shinsegae, one of South Korea's biggest high-end department-store operators, same-store sales rose 15% from a year earlier in August, according to Bank of America, with luxury sales up 20%. Revenue from international customers jumped 82%. The strength fits a pattern BofA has found in past market cycles. Korean department-store sales tend to follow increases in household equity investment, with the relationship strongest at a lag of about a year. Luxury companies are seeing strong demand, too. LVMH reported strong first-half growth in Asia outside Japan. CEO Bernard Arnault highlighted the "remarkable performance" of Louis Vuitton's new stores in Seoul and Beijing as one factor behind faster growth in the second quarter. Richemont, the owner of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, also reported strong demand. Asia-Pacific sales rose 21% in the quarter ended June, with South Korea and Taiwan among its strongest markets. But the latest numbers suggest the spending boom is cooling after a blockbuster first half that sent both luxury sales and shares of South Korea's major department-store operators soaring alongside the broader market. "Demand is no longer uniformly strong, but it is not breaking either," JPMorgan analysts wrote in a September 18 report. Luxury demand had cooled since July as market volatility increased, with jewelry, watches, and top-tier brands holding up better than the broader category, the analysts added. Stock-market gains are only one way the AI boom is reaching Korean households. Morgan Stanley now expects the country's semiconductor windfall to spread more broadly through investment, government finances, and household income. "Korea is poised to monetize the semis super-cycle on a scale and with durability of historic proportions," its economists wrote, saying the benefits could spread through the economy over the next three to five years. Morgan Stanley estimates Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix could generate 66.7 trillion won, or $49 billion, in combined gross employee compensation this year, rising to 107.6 trillion won in 2027 and 114.9 trillion won in 2028. Average annual liquid bonus capacity between 2026 and 2028 could be about 20 times the 2025 level, the bank added. That leaves another source of spending power even if stock-market gains become less reliable. Japan's high-end retailers are also seeing affluent domestic shoppers spend as the country's stock market has also rallied strongly this year, with AI-linked chip and equipment makers among the biggest winners. At Takashimaya, one of Japan's largest high-end department-store chains, in-store sales rose 3.9% in August from a year earlier. Meanwhile, Richemont's sales in Japan surged 36% in the quarter ended June, driven by both domestic customers and tourists. Hermès reported an 11% increase in first-half Japanese sales at constant exchange rates. Biswas said the AI wealth effect is likely to be more muted in Japan. "The majority of Japanese households have low direct exposure to the stock market, with a strong focus on low-risk fixed income assets," he said. Taiwan offers a longer-running example. Around Hsinchu Science Park — home to TSMC and hundreds of companies in its semiconductor supply chain — years of chip wealth have fueled demand for housing, luxury retail, and premium services. The US economy looks like it's headed for a spell of weakness, a veteran strategist is warning. Jim Paulsen, a Wall Street economist and the former chief investment strategist at the Leuthold Group, sees a troubling trajectory ahead for the US, with the economy likely to see weak growth going forward, pressured by a "cocktail of past contractionary forces" acting on the economy, he wrote on his Substack this week. Paulsen said he created a new gauge to measure tightness of financial conditions, pointing to how accommodative or restrictive the broader macro backdrop is for growth. The Leading Financial Conditions Gauge measures five economic policies and three economic forces. It has proven to be a leading indicator of economic growth and stock prices, Paulsen said, citing his analysis of the gauge's swings dating back to 1970. Of the eight indicators in the model, seven represent a contractionary force on the economy, Paulsen said. Here's the rundown of the gauge's contractionary signals: Paulsen's gauge of market and economic conditions currently sits in its topmost quartile, signaling that financial conditions are tight. Historically, every major recession in the US has been preceded by the gauge rising to that level, he said. Paulsen questioned whether the Fed should raise interest rates further from current levels. Central bankers, though, have come out with hawkish comments on the outlook for monetary policy in recent weeks, and markets see two more Fed rate hikes by year-end.  "My guess is it will prove to be a mistake that the Fed became more restrictive 'after' the Leading Financial Conditions Gauge just surged to its most contractionary quartile. Expect weaker economic growth, rising recession fears (although probably no actual recession), lower—not higher—bond yields, and a more challenging stock market in the coming months," Paulsen wrote. When are we going to stop counting out Mark Zuckerberg? As concerns over AI mounted over the summer, Meta was one of the companies hit hardest. Investors were particularly skeptical about the firm's massive capex-spending plans, especially since Meta was seen as more concentrated on AI than fellow hyperscalers like Microsoft. But the roaring success of Muse, Meta's new personal AI agent, has ignited a whole new discussion about AI use cases ("musecases," anyone?) It's also shed light on which parts of the market could win or lose in an era of agentic growth. Let's start with Meta itself. The company's stock is at its highest level since last October, up 19% since Muse launched on Sept. 8. Much of that came Monday, when it soared 11% after Muse hit No. 1 on Apple's App Store over the weekend. Meta's more zoomed-out stock chart is remarkably choppy. It seems that no matter how many times shares get knocked down, Zuck always has another ace up his sleeve. But it's important to note that the success of Muse so far has been based on rapid consumer adoption. Turning that into revenue is another story. At this point, investors are betting Meta can turn its enormous user base and app ecosystem into a lucrative new business. Muse's breakout comes as Meta Connect — the company's annual developer conference — begins today, giving the company a chance to address the fervor and tease what comes next. Meta's goal is to turn Muse into a new revenue stream beyond advertising. The basic version is free, but the company already offers $20- and $100-a-month tiers for heavier users. Its next challenge will be convincing people to hand over the reins of their lives — and pay for the privilege. After all, Muse doesn't just collect data. It can enter apps and websites to handle tasks like shopping, making travel plans, and writing emails. It could end up being a tough sell for Meta, which is such a lightning rod that its controversies become Hollywood movies. Chipmakers have been pulled along for the ride this week, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index up more than 6% in just two days. Zooming in on the sector, there was a clear divide. On the winning side were CPU-exposed companies (Intel, AMD, Arm, etc.) whose products serve as the all-purpose brains that run software and coordinate tasks. GPU-makers like Nvidia, meanwhile, struggled to get as much of a lift. They've been the darling of the AI trade to date, with a premium placed on their ability to crunch massive amounts of data at once. Elsewhere in the tech space — judging by stock moves this week — cloud infrastructure, networking, cybersecurity, payments, and e-commerce are expected to be beneficiaries of a further agentic push. Shopify in particular has been on a tear after announcing a deal to integrate Muse with Shop Pay. The losers are less obvious, as there hasn't been a broad agentic-led sell-off. But one strategic loser could be Amazon, which blocked Muse from shopping on its platform. The company's shares are basically flat for the week. The episode highlights potential market risk for closed e-commerce ecosystems. There are also businesses that could be replaced by automation, including online travel agencies, insurance brokers, and comparison-shopping sites. If AI handles the clerical dirty work, the middleman may no longer be necessary. Muse is another reminder that Meta can still turn a skeptical market on its head. Citi is the latest company outside Madison Avenue to launch an advertising business. The bank exclusively told CMO Insider that it's creating a new unit called Citi Commerce Media, which will let brands advertise to its more than 70 million customers based on their spending. Citi will target ads to people on its own app and website, as well as on other properties, based on their spending histories. So a customer scrolling on Facebook could see a 10% off ad from a travel company, for instance. Part of Citi's pitch is that it can link its ads to measurable business impacts. It said it ran a pilot ad with retail, payments, technology, and health and beauty brands. Two campaigns produced an average 15% lift in spending compared to people who weren't shown ads. Citi said its platform would be informed by intel from 6.5 billion annual transactions across more than 700 spending categories. "We are focusing primarily based on your spending pattern, and that's what the advertisers care the most about," said Abhinav Anand, head of value cards, lending, and commerce at Citi. A growing number of non-advertising companies have leveraged their customers' data to build ad businesses. Citi is an example of the fast-growing field of financial media networks, in which firms use first-party customer data to enable advertisers to target audiences across the digital ecosystem. As financial institutions, they have a fuller picture of their customers' spending than typical retail media networks, where retailers — often grocers or big-box stores like Walmart — run ads based on data about how people browse and spend within their ecosystems. Anand said he sees an opportunity to take spending share from retail media networks that have more limited data. By 5 am every morning, Emma Waters is on the sofa with a blanket, plotting America’s baby-making future. For two hours, she stays off her phone, inspired by Deep Work, the self-help bestseller. At 7:30, she does emails. Waters, 28 years old, is a monk of productivity who makes motherhood look like all-­natural Adderall. At 8 am, it’s time for breakfast and the Bible. Waters tries to live her life according to the mantra “Love God, get married, have babies.” She asks that I not use the real names of her two daughters for their safety, even though they’ve been printed elsewhere. I’ll call them Gertie and Ophelia, which are close enough. All morning, they play. Ophelia, the baby, runs around in white tights, shirtless, clutching a pink purse; Gertie’s doll won’t stop crying. Jack, Waters’ husband, flits in and out. There isn’t much to say about Jack, other than that he’s hot, is studying to be a preacher, and has a big desk at home, much bigger than Waters’, featuring a bust of Nietzsche. In the same room, Waters has a pull-out secretary where she takes meetings, not far from a portrait of a glowering President Trump. The only thing Waters doesn’t really do is exercise; she hasn’t found the time. Not many people outside of DC have heard of Waters, who mostly works from home in a dreary Pennsylvania suburb named after a long-offshored manufacturer. Yet Waters is a factory for policy papers and op-eds extolling the harms of unregulated reproductive technology, probing the moral issues that liberals don’t want to touch with a 10-foot turkey baster. At least once a month, reporting on fertility, I ask for an academic source and am instead directed to Waters, author of a biblical women’s leadership book that basically says the best thing about the Barbie movie was the patriarchy. Emma Waters, her husband Jackson, and their two daughters. The craziest thing is that, in certain ways, she’s a voice of reason. America’s $10 billion fertility industry is suffering a massive PR crisis that makes the embryo mix-ups and baby-selling schemes of yore seem quaint. A few recent headlines: “The Chinese Billionaires Having Dozens of US-Born Babies Via Surrogate,” “The Family Law Loophole That Lets Sex Offenders Parent Kids,” “California Couple Busted for Running Suspected Baby Mill,” “Surrogate Mother Who Refused to Abort Baby Gives Birth Amid Ongoing Legal Dispute.” Polygenic testing companies promise today’s parents that they can pick the tallest, smartest, least-bald offspring, mainstreaming debates about the “Black-white IQ gap.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman—a father via surrogacy—and Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong are invested in an embryo-editing startup. If you believe what they told The Wall Street Journal, their first gene-hacked baby has probably already been born. Many right-wing techies are jazzed about these developments, which might bump up birth rates or create “better” spawn. Many liberals don’t know how to talk about the ethical pitfalls. Emma Waters fills in the gaps. As a kind of backroom wheeler-dealer and political strategist, she is the mastermind behind Florida’s recent ban on international surrogacy, the Texas GOP’s souring on IVF, and the squashing of Trump’s “fertilization president” initiatives. This God-loving, JD Vance–stanning Gen Z-er might be standing between you and your ability to have a family, or she might be, somehow, the force that makes it possible. Waters has so much to teach us about optics and politics and why, in so many arenas, Democrats are losing so dramatically. Waters wants to dismantle fertility as we know it. And she wants to do it politely, during nap time, with her husband’s permission. Waters wasn’t always political. She and her three younger siblings were homeschooled by their mother in a poor, rural part of southern Georgia, while their father worked 60-hour weeks as a facilities manager and HVAC repairman. (Waters describes her local high school as the kind of place where one-third of students got chlamydia.) Growing up, Waters never felt aligned with either party: Republicans praised free trade and cheap widgets; Democrats pushed equal pay and shoved kids into day care. Then, in her junior year at a Christian college in Tennessee, Waters heard a podcast interview with JD Vance. “Everything he says, I relate to,” she remembers thinking. When she graduated a year later, in 2021—as valedictorian—she applied for an internship at American Moment, a training ground of sorts for rising conservatives. They gave her a full-time job. Around this time, she met Jackson Waters at a mock-government event. Emma recounts their “whirlwind romance” in her book, Lead Like Jael. After “a summer of tense conversations,” she broke up with him “on a whim.” She wanted a career in politics; the thought of being a wife and mother felt like “a major letdown.” With the help of a pastor, she realized she only had these notions because of girlboss feminism. She begged Jack to take her back and got married at 24. She was an anomaly even among Republicans. Waters had heard older colleagues refer to women who got married at that age as “child brides.” “Take up your ladle like a sword,” Waters writes in her book. “Stand behind your stove like a sentinel.” Waters loved life in DC: walking 24,000 steps a day, getting coffee with everyone and their mom, hosting dinners in her basement. When she got pregnant with Gertie, she and Jack wanted to prove that life didn’t end with a baby. But she needed a job with more flexibility that would eventually allow Jack to attend in-person seminary. In 2022, Waters approached the Heritage Foundation, the most influential conservative think tank. Heritage had recently shed its intellectual bona fides to become a MAGA mouthpiece; the next year, it would release Project 2025, the playbook for Trump 2.0. Waters pitched Heritage that she would cover emerging fertility tech as an analyst: crafting policy briefs, penning op-eds, whispering into politicians’ ears. Waters found traditional pro-life policy banal—everything was about abortion. Debates around IVF started and ended with “Are embryos people?” She wanted to apply her dual major in political science and biblical studies to cutting-edge science. At the time, it seemed like “the least popular policy issue,” she says, but she promised the bosses it would soon be a big deal. They were sold. Waters found her conservative colleagues ignorant about the state of assisted baby-making. One Hill staffer emailed Waters about a test that counts embryos’ chromosomes, asking, “Will this be around in 10 years?” It had been around for decades. At that point, a Chinese scientist had already embryo-­Crispr’d babies, gone to jail for it, and gotten out. Sex selection had become a standard part of American IVF; the first sex-selected people were in their thirties. It was easier to open a surrogacy agency than an ice cream cart or a tanning salon. Then there was China. In 2023, more than two years before mainstream media outlets reported on Sino-US infant import-exports, Waters was on Fox News, accompanied by an article headlined “Chinese ‘Rent-a-Womb’ Industry Using American Surrogates Is a National Security Threat.” She called it “the new face of birth tourism.” Intended parents didn’t even have to leave the country. Our nation’s lax laws meant that you could ship sperm over and get an American citizen shipped back. Nobody wants to talk about women in tech anymore—not even women in tech. Is that progress? Waters hates it when people harp on what she’s anti. Instead, she wants people to focus on what she’s pro: pro-“human flourishing”; pro-“the human person,” including embryos; pro-man-woman marriage; pro-life (duh); pro-Natural Procreative Technology, by which infertile heteros of breeding age clean up their diets, reduce their plastics, and ultimately get knocked up according to God’s will. Pronatalist? She prefers “pro-family,” which implies more straight marriages where straight penises and vaginas produce tons of babies. (Critics would add that the goal is really white Christian babies.) Waters never says she’s against IVF per se. She doesn’t talk about “murdering” embryos; she makes it sound more like negligent manslaughter. She mostly argues that IVF doesn’t work. It encourages young women to postpone their true calling by falsely reassuring them that there’s still time. To Waters, IVF is the conduit for many horrors. Ranking and selecting embryos tricks parents into thinking they can choose and control what kind of children they have, cheapening God’s handmade gift into an off-brand dustmop plucked off an Amazon wish list. It allows you to outsource reproduction to surrogates, objectifying women and commoditizing babies. Decoupling sex, marriage, and procreation distorts the natural order. Infertility explodes. Civilizations collapse. In her work, Waters fastidiously avoids mentioning gays, singles, or women over 40. When I ask her about this omission, she gets defensive: “It’s not about the desires of adults. It’s about the rights and well-being of children.” Waters is a Republican, but that doesn’t mean all Republicans agree with her. The vast majority of Republicans support IVF as is. The pronatalist movement has two factions, the tech right and the trads. The tech right sees artificial wombs, surrogacy, and genetic optimization as tools to boost birth rates. Trads, like Waters, think these things will make the problem worse. Besides China, nothing rankles Waters like embryo screening tools that promise to let parents “have your best baby.” Nobody really expects these so-called polygenic tests to move into the mainstream or ever become very accurate, but they set the tone for a future where parents can edit their children’s genes. On X, Noor Siddiqui, CEO of the startup Orchid and one of Waters’ least favorite founders, wastes no time in shaming breeders who fail to optimize. Getting knocked up the old-fashioned way is irresponsible: “What if your baby never walks?” Siddiqui has posted. “What if they’re never able to live independently? What if you could have stopped it … but chose not to?” (Stopping it, in this case, means making sure your disabled child isn’t born.) “Just be honest: You’re OK with your kid potentially suffering for life so you can feel morally superior, or because you can’t be inconvenienced.” In a decade, Siddiqui warns, all babies will be born using IVF and her test—Waters’ definition of dystopia. Like many at Heritage, Waters was disappointed when Trump included free IVF in his 2024 platform, later declaring himself the “father of IVF” and “the fertilization president.” But Waters still found fertile ground (sorry) filled with low-hanging fruit. There were zero federal regulations governing surrogacy—she would shepherd the first one. “We have model legislation to SHUT DOWN foreign nations who rent the wombs of American women,” she wrote on X. She would rail against the creepy, unpopular polygenic tests that are opposed by every professional society. With the nation’s most influential conservative organization backing her, she’d push to mainstream so-called restorative reproductive medicine that co-opted the language of social justice while addressing the root causes of women’s broken, barren bodies. Last November, waters sat onstage at the Heritage Foundation wearing a faux leather dress, slouchy boots, and a periwinkle double-breasted blazer while dozens of protesters in red Handmaid’s Tale cloaks screamed on the sidewalk outside. I’d come to DC to meet Waters in person. It was a tough week for the organization. Its president had taken heat, and nearly had to resign, for defending Tucker Carlson’s choice to platform Nick Fuentes, a white supremacist. (Fuentes: “Hitler was awesome. Hitler was right. And the Holocaust didn’t happen.”) I wondered if there were always a dozen cops outside of the building. Sometimes the roar and the sirens were so deafening it was hard to hear Waters, but the disturbance seemed to make her smile. First, Waters warmed up the room by having a “chat” with a mom who gets told by libs that she should’ve aborted her disabled son. Then Waters turned to the main event. “Welcome, gentlemen,” she said. She had assembled four white experts for “Editing Destiny,” a panel on the subject of polygenic tests and gene editing. Two seemed like MAGA partisans. Two were legitimate academics. Waters had the energy of a high school newspaper reporter with a blowout and makeup that perfectly concealed her prominent chin. Everyone agreed that somatic gene editing on “born people” was good. Waters pointed out how it served the MAHA goal to eliminate disease at the source. But germline gene editing, the panel also agreed, was risky and unnecessary. No one said “fetus” or “God”; instead they evoked “the human person” and “flourishing.” Ben Hurlbut, one of the academics, made a moving, secular argument against polygenic selection. This was the “first relational act” you make with your future children, he told me, and it invites a serious rift. Around the room, young female staffers in tight dresses held microphones for Q&A. The panel took a few questions. One attendee noted the harms of Tylenol. After the event, Waters introduced me to Austin Rogers, then general counsel to Florida senator Rick Scott. Rogers wore a green Rolex with his hair gelled up in the front—he wouldn’t have looked out of place at a nightclub. Rogers told me they were using Waters’ model legislation to try to ban surrogacy from “foreign adversaries.” He was looking for a Democratic partner. He mentioned the latest story, covered by every major outlet, of a Chinese couple in California who had commissioned at least 25 surrogates to carry their children—a perfectly legal scheme—only to allegedly abuse most of those children in a mansion. He said, “I read it and my hair was on fire.” That night, I walked Hurlbut, the academic, back to the train station and asked him why he agreed to speak at the Heritage Foundation. It wasn’t about party politics, he said. These issues couldn’t be split cleanly into left and right. “Anyone taking this seriously is creating a service to the public discourse,” he said. I asked who the big players were on the liberal side. “Big players? There are no big players. Just a few voices crying in the wilderness.” Two months later, I visit Waters at home, in the type of town where hotels keep their lobby doors locked at all times. “I’ll have lunch to share with you,” Waters emails. When I arrive, she is wearing heeled boots and trendy jeans, making a butternut squash soup with bacon and brie. Ophelia watches from her high chair, wearing white tights underneath a fancy outfit. Over the next 27 hours, Waters will serve her husband and me a parade of elaborate orange foods: frittata with broken spaghetti, clementines, clam chowder (yes, also orange). (The girls will also eat Cheez-Its, Goldfish, and chicken nuggets.) I recognize her hospitality tactics from Lead Like Jael, specifically the chapter titled “Motherhood as Warfare.” Waters advises women to embrace distinctly feminine means of influence. “No woman in the Bible picked up a sword to fight,” she tells me. Waters named her book after a biblical matriarch who offered an enemy commander a place to stay and then pierced his head with a tent peg, thus winning the battle. I fear I am the enemy commander in this story. In the book, Waters urges: “Take up your ladle like a sword. Stand behind your stove like a sentinel.” Waters’ book was published in March. Her house is modest yet beautiful, full of damask furniture. Christmas cards ring the kitchen doorway. In one photo, Simone and Malcolm Collins, the prominent pronatalist couple who embrace the term “hipster eugenicists,” smile from behind thick black glasses. On the credenza next to the dining room table, there’s a gilded Bible, a Venetian clock, and a ring light that never turns off. Jack, home for lunch, says grace. Even 13-month-old Ophelia clasps her hands, closes her eyes, and bows her head. Waters gets things done by being very, very nice. Simone Collins tells me, “I don’t know a single person in the pronatalist movement who doesn’t like Emma. She’s golden.” Even though the Collinses promote polygenic testing, IVF, and surrogacy, Waters considers them friends and makes a point not to publicly criticize them. In any given hour, Waters laser-focuses on a single issue. Another conservative tells me, “She could do an event with someone on Tuesday and be on the opposite side of a protest on Friday.” When she gets into a flame war with someone on X, she invites them to collaborate. That’s how she secured the special guest for today’s Zoom working group: the founder of a polygenic testing company. One Tuesday a month, during nap time, Waters hosts private discussions with a group of bioethicists, activists, and policy wonks. Many potential collaborators do not want to be associated with Heritage, so Waters does much of her work in secret. She paraphrases a sign that Ronald Reagan kept on his desk in the Oval Office: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.” In the glow of the ring light, Waters and I huddle around her dining room table. I’m allowed to join if I don’t name names: I recognize a few prominent pro-lifers, and one or two liberals. “There is no dispute about how the technology works,” the polygenic testing founder says. He hammers home that two papers a day are being written about the associations between genes. His vibe oscillates between nerd and evil professor. He repeats at least a dozen times that his technology works. “There are ideologues masquerading as experts. You can easily fool a WIRED reporter into writing into her story that it doesn’t work.” Waters asks a question about “children who have been born already.” Then someone asks about a recent paper showing that the sibling with the tallest-seeming genes is actually only the tallest about 25 percent of the time. This implies that, three out of four times, “picking the tallest baby,” well, wouldn’t work. The founder is irritated. One person might be predicted to be taller by 1 centimeter, but the error bars are 2 centimeters. “Falling within the error bars of the model means it’s successful,” the founder says. Waters chimes in: “If the solution from a polygenic risk score for breast cancer was euthanasia, people would have a problem with it.” Then, she adds with a smirk, “That’s probably already happening in Canada.” To Waters, embryos are “human people”—but she won’t belabor the point or argue about metaphysical priors. The founder reminds us, “If you want to call it eugenics, you can, but don’t say it doesn’t work.” Many of Waters’ critics dismiss her as a fool because of her retrograde gender views, which underpin all her other ideas. I read Lead Like Jael in one sitting; my eyes got dry from popping so far out of my head. “There’s a hierarchy in marriage,” Waters writes. She advises her readers to become “good at being a woman” by “cultivating distinctly feminine strengths,” such as good posture. In an analysis of Greta Gerwig’s Barbie movie, patriarchy was “the first real innovation,” she writes. “Strong and godly men propel society forward.” Waters analyzes how, in the official portraits of First Lady Melania Trump, even her nails and eyebrows focus on the greater mission. She urges readers to redefine success as a joint pursuit, beginning with a husband’s career. Parents should start talking about marriage and motherhood at the same age as they ask kids what they want to be when they grow up. Women’s work should be flexible and easy to pause: “To neglect the home to pursue work is to invert God’s design.” Women are there to “support and strengthen” but not replace men. “Rightful authority” begins with husbands in the home. Women can lead, but only about 8 percent of the time. Sitting in a trendy café, radiant in a puffy-sleeved red sweater and an Oura ring, Waters explains to me that the difference between men and women goes back to Genesis. Adam’s names mean “ground” and “man.” Eve’s names mean “fire,” “woman,” “mother.” So men are supposed to dig holes while women launch rockets? No: “A man is pulled toward the ground,” Waters says. “The wife is pulled to her husband and her children.” Waters tries to live her life according to the mantra “Love God, get married, have babies.” She goes on: “We don’t want to go back to the 1950s. God put us in our time for a reason.” Still, there’s a lot to learn from the halcyon days when all 50 states allowed marital rape. Waters explains that the problem with the 1950s was that technology, like the dishwasher, stripped women of meaningful labor. “What would have been amazing is if women had radically rethought what they could do with the time they’d been given”—instead of just turning to wage labor. Despite providing most of the childcare, working full-time, and supporting her husband through school, Waters claims that balancing work and motherhood hasn’t been that hard. (Waters isn’t even so hot on federal paid family leave, since it encourages moms to go back to work.) Here’s where I admit that Waters and I have more in common than I could have imagined. I got married at 25. I love being married and raising my child. We both go to church every Sunday (though mine has a gay pastor). I find it sad how young people see pregnancy as a funeral dirge for their hopes and dreams. I, too, expect low birth rates to cause big problems, and I suspect many “childfree” people will experience regret in 20 years. I’m inspired by Waters, how she cranked out more than 150 policy papers, interviews, and op-eds while I wrote this measly profile. I’m jealous of the time she spends with her daughters and how well behaved they are and how she managed to travel alone with a 4-month-old to Hungary to speak at a conference. But when Waters tells me that once you become a wife you have to subjugate yourself to your husband, it’s hard to keep a straight face. If she wants to boost marriage rates, I ask, wouldn’t egalitarian partnership be an easier sell? She doesn’t have an answer. “It never crossed my mind.” There’s a glaring gap between what Waters professes—that a woman’s highest calling is the home—and what she does, which is support her family financially while being way more influential and successful than her husband. She reconciles this by, literally, doing it all, while swearing she will slow down her career at a moment’s notice. By that same token, it’s also hard to distinguish between what Waters really thinks, what she is supposed to say, what’s rage-bait, and if there’s any meaningful difference between those categories. Her X background used to be a photo of “What’s Wrong With ‘Equal Rights’ for Women?” by Phyllis Schlafly, an activist who started speeches by thanking her husband for allowing her to be there. When I ask her about it, Waters says, “If your enemies think you’re oppressed, play up the trope.” On the right, optics are everything. “How you project yourself is a political message,” Waters says. Before coming to DC, she had eight piercings, including belly button and eyebrow rings, but she didn’t want to be perceived like that. “Your appearance shows what you value,” she says. “I really value dressing well and pleasing my husband.” If Waters had her way, there might be some IVF, but it wouldn’t involve ranking, destroying, or indefinitely freezing embryos. The only lawful surrogacy would be altruistic for heterosexual married couples with a documented history of infertility. (The gays, singles, and AOCs of the world would, in other words, put children’s well-being first and just not have them.) In an international context, some of Waters’ views are perfectly normal. Almost every wealthy country besides the US bans elective sex selection. Every other wealthy country bans commercial surrogacy, which the UN called a form of violence against women and “the sale of children.” UN committees see anonymous gamete donation as incompatible with children’s rights. Most Western countries require tests to undergo some kind of approval process before going to market, so polygenic tests are out. In Germany, parents need government approval to genetically test embryos. Through a global lens, American Big Fertility is bizarro. But for Democrats, it’s often seen as too politically toxic to criticize the largely unregulated industry. Challenging almost anything about it—even just that private-equity-backed clinics conduct most IVF cycles—opens the door for critics like Waters. Businesses have framed picking the sex of your baby, or even picking your Aryan-est baby, as a matter of “reproductive autonomy” on par with abortion. Lefties who disagree mostly keep their mouths shut. It’s almost too easy for Waters. Google will send anyone disturbed by the status quo straight to her op-eds. While Waters invites journalists to her home and cooks them elaborate meals, some fertility professionals blame the reporters who dissect the scandals. After I wrote about a surrogacy gone wrong last year, Ron Poole-Dayan, the executive director of Men Having Babies, told me, “You are the problem. Journalists like you are a big part of the reason gay men can’t have families.” People working in assisted reproduction see so many happy stories of family formation, they don’t even seem to understand what the problem is. At a recent conference for a surrogacy and egg donation ethics group, one attendee remarked, “An airplane takes off and lands a thousand times, and no one writes a story. A plane crashes once—everyone writes about it.” Someone else chimed in, “And flying is safer than driving!” At the conference, surrounded by attorneys and professionals who seemed earnestly invested in doing the right thing, I thought of the left’s purity test problem: wanting so badly to be 100 percent correct that you forget how you look; ceding the hard topics to your opponents, who can wrap a kernel of truth in a bundle of nonsense; getting defensive when you could’ve invited the enemy in for a bowl of orange soup. The biggest criticism lobbed at Waters is, obviously, that she wants to turn America into The Handmaid’s Tale. The second biggest criticism is that she’s a hypocrite. Waters’ kids aren’t in day care, but that doesn’t mean she doesn’t have help. At Waters’ house, I was surprised to meet a relative who consoled sobbing dolls and occupied the children while Waters entertained me and Jack studied the Bible or whatever. Waters’ mom is also a “full-time grandma” to Gertie and Ophelia. The third biggest criticism is, let’s say, her credentials. “She’s not an academic. She’s not someone who actually has experience in these things,” says Lauren Hall, a political science professor at Rochester Institute of Technology. The feminist writer Jessica Valenti has essentially called Waters a failed influencer. It’s not easy being an influential conservative mom who tells other moms of young kids to stay home. Criticisms of the Heritage Foundation, meanwhile, come from both the left and right. It’s “the worst-case scenario for a woman,” says Hall. She says Heritage puts “token” women forward, who have to hew to “a very particular party line.” In early 2025, an anonymous staff member sent letters to Heritage trustees alleging discrimination against childless women. Waters disagrees, of course—she’s a fierce defender of Heritage. “America first,” she tells me. “MASS DEPORTATIONS NOW!” she tweets. She admits that Nick Fuentes says some “disgusting” things and describes him as “a young white man” who was “disenfranchised by the Republican Party because he dared to question our relationship with Israel.” When I ask her about the GOP’s unofficial strategy of “no enemies to the right,” a big-tent welcome for neo-Nazis and white nationalists, she snaps back, “Don’t you think the left is the same? Normalizing pedophilia. Abortion until birth. Rampant antisemitism … Why do you think Josh Shapiro wasn’t the vice presidential nominee?” Waters’ master plan to undermine the fertility industry seems to be working. In November 2025, Senator Rick Scott proposed the SAFE KIDS Act, banning citizens of “hostile foreign regimes” from participating in surrogacy. In Florida, a similar law passed at the state level in May. At the start of 2026, Florida attorney general James Uthmeier stepped in to try to get two French dads un-recognized as their son’s legal parents, calling surrogacy “unconstitutional” and “modern-day slavery.” In July, Uthmeier intervened in another case, arguing that Florida should ignore an intended parent’s California parentage order, seemingly in opposition to the Full Faith and Credit clause of the Constitution. A proposed bill in Kentucky would ban all commercial surrogacy. When Trump called himself “the father of IVF” in 2024, it looked like Waters had lost the battle against petri dish kids. But in June, Texas’ GOP denounced the procedure, and Trump has thus far reneged on his promises to make it free. In a recent grant application, the Department of Health and Human Services called frozen embryos “children.” Many observers tell me they think Waters’ work is “the driving force” in pushing fertility regulation out of the fringes and into the mainstream. They also tell me the new laws are insincere and bad, fraught with unintended consequences. For example, the Florida attorney general’s anti-surrogacy argument would seem to prohibit Evangelicals’ sacred cow, adoption. Courts may challenge some of these laws in the coming months and years, but there’s no denying that American baby-­making is going trad. On August 6, Trump issued executive orders banning birth tourism and denying passports to surrogate babies with foreign parents—measures proposed by Waters. Her star continues to rise. Waters got a second book deal earlier this year (working title: Rethinking Fertility) and is contributing to a documentary about cryopreservation called Frozen Orphans. She recently presented at a Harvard summit on embryo law and ethics; four of the 20 other speakers have referenced Waters in their work. She is not opposed to running for office, although of course it will have to wait until her kids are older. In early September, she gave birth to her third child: another girl. AI glasses shipments more than doubled to 4.2 million in the first half of 2026, Omdia says, and Meta shipped four pairs in five. The vendor in second place sells glasses with no camera. The count arrives as Meta prepares to show a camera-free pair at Connect, and as the rules on camera glasses tighten. As scrutiny of camera-equipped AI glasses intensifies, tighter privacy settings and clearer messaging will not be enough. Jason Low, research director at Omdia, said that on Tuesday. The research firm had just published its count of the AI glasses market for the first half of 2026. Companies must define exactly what always-on cameras capture, he said. They must also show users how that content is used, and guarantee it never reaches third parties. Omdia published the numbers the day before Meta’s Connect conference, where the company is expected to show a camera-free pair. The numbers also show a split at the top of the market. The leader sells glasses with a camera. The vendor in second place sells a pair without one. Global AI glasses shipments reached 4.2 million units in the first half of the year, according to Omdia. That is up 127% on the same period of 2025. The firm called AI glasses an emerging category, with growth stabilising as the market expands from a very low base. It also said the sector faces a more complex environment. Omdia pointed to intensifying competition across different frame designs, and to mounting scrutiny over user privacy. Omdia’s own chart puts the half below the second half of 2025, when shipments reached 6.5 million. The United States took 53.7% of the total and grew 103% year on year. Mainland China came second, with 12.3%. Qiran Ju, a senior analyst at Omdia, credited Meta’s momentum and a wave of new entrants from China. He also named the features that sell the devices. Just as critically, vendors have made the value proposition immediately clear to buyers by focusing on hands-free photo and video capture, open-ear audio, and AI assistance within everyday frames. Meta shipped 3.4 million AI glasses in the half, for an 81.3% share of the market, Omdia said. Even Realities climbed from fifth place in the second half of 2025 to second. It shipped 102,000 units, a 2.4% share. Omdia put that down to demand for its G2 series across North America and Western Europe. Omdia’s vendor chart names Alibaba next, with 2.1%. The G2 has neither a camera nor speakers. Ju described the choice this way. Even Realities takes a different frame design from most AI glasses. By removing both the camera and speakers, and focusing instead on a slimmer design, a small monochrome display and productivity features such as real-time transcription, it shows how vendors are exploring different ways to make AI glasses useful in everyday life. Even Realities is not alone in that bet. Halliday relaunched with a camera-free pair aimed at meetings in July. Shipments in mainland China rose 306% year on year to 520,000 units. Omdia described the country as the main supply chain hub for the devices. It also called China a testbed for new combinations of display, camera and audio. No vendor dominates there. Alibaba led with 17.4%, INMO took 14.6% and Xiaomi 14.0%. The three together accounted for 46.1% of shipments, against Meta’s 81.3% of the global market. What we are seeing in China provides early but definitive signs that there is no single, one-size-fits-all solution in the AI glasses space. Low said privacy, alongside varied user preferences, is a major driver of that fragmentation. Beijing has its own rules in progress, and wants a light on the glasses whenever they record. The Information reported on 15 September that Meta plans camera-free glasses, codenamed Luna, citing people familiar with the matter. According to the report, the model has six built-in microphones. They let the wearer talk to Meta AI and to Muse, the company’s new AI agent. It also has a button on the side to call up Meta AI, and speakers similar to those in the current models. Meta is targeting October for shipments, The Information reported. Reuters, which carried the report, said Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment. TNW covered the Luna report the same week. Mark Zuckerberg’s Connect keynote starts at 4pm Pacific time on Wednesday. Meta has not confirmed the product. The pressure on camera glasses has moved from complaints to rules. Western Australia this week banned smart glasses from every public school, and councils in Sydney, Brisbane and Melbourne have barred them from pools. Omdia listed hands-free photo and video capture first among the features driving sales. Some analysts told Reuters on Wednesday they doubt a camera-free model can allay privacy concerns about devices that can still record audio. They also said dropping the camera could blunt demand, since photo and video capture ranks among the most popular features. Analysts also expect Meta to show a new camera-equipped Ray-Ban model at Connect, Reuters reported. SonicEdge makes miniaturised audio components for wearables and smartphones, so it has a direct stake in glasses built around microphones and speakers. Its chief executive, Moti Margalit, said in a statement sent to TNW that Meta is investing heavily because it does not want to lose control of the voice-based interface. We naturally talk to people, so why not talk to our glasses? If Meta ships Luna in October, the first camera-free pair from the market leader will fall inside Omdia’s count for the second half of 2026. Last year, that half came to 6.5 million units. 7/10 Every bird enthusiast has probably heard of Birdfy and Birdbuddy smart bird feeders, but a handful of competitors have quietly been refining their models over multiple generations—to the point where they’re starting to outpace the OGs in engineering, features, and design. Kiwibit is one of them. I tested Kiwibit’s first feeder, the Beako, in mid-2025 and was impressed by its robust plastic body, removable dual-sided seed reservoir, and three-minute video captures—there was nothing quite like it at the time, and almost all of its features were available sans subscription. However, the optional rooftop solar panel stopped working after six weeks, which kept it from being a pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders. The Beako’s subsequent update, the Feeder 2, made the solar panel standard on all units, upped the panel’s output from 4.4 to 5 watts, and fixed the longevity issue—it’s currently my top pick for Best Design. The Feeder 2 Pro, meanwhile, has totally redone the camera to offer phase detection autofocus (PDAF) in 4K HDR—one of the most impressive smart feeder hardware offerings on the market. The companion app upgrade, however, still has some kinks to work out. I tested the Feeder 2 Pro for a total of four weeks: one week at the non-subscription tier, and three weeks with Kiwibit Plus (also alternately referred to as “Family Premium” or “Premium Family), which at $90 a year offers AI ID, 60-day cloud recording (the feeder also supports microSD storage up to 512 GB), and new gallery views and roundup reports. Without a subscription, camera quality is the same (some other feeder brands, like Birdbuddy, will paywall higher resolution), but here you’re limited to a bare-bones feed of video captures, and there’s no AI ID to sort or identify them—you’ll have to look at every image to make sure you didn’t miss anything interesting. This can be especially laborious if the same bird visits 15 times or more per day, especially since the camera placement means the thumbnails often show only the top of the bird’s head, if they show anything. This is atypical for a feeder with an MSRP of $290—most models at this price point include a lifetime subscription. Thankfully, it is still easy to download and share 8-MP images and videos, and the camera records as long as the bird is there—up to three minutes—to ensure no movements are missed. The PDAF works to minimize blur and ensure all features are sharp. At various points during my test, I did notice the motion of the lens zooming in and out being clocked by multiple birds, who either immediately stopped eating to watch the camera warily or flew away. It didn’t happen often enough for me to wish the feature didn’t exist, but it is something to consider if your local birds are easily spooked. The subscription gives you the same feed of video captures, but with labels of the bird species so you can skip past the ones that aren’t worth opening. There’s also a tile view under “Visits” that shows which birds have visited over the feeder’s lifetime and when they were last seen. However, this is only so useful given that the AI ID is wrong a hefty percentage of the time—fish crows, Cape May warblers, mangrove warblers, red fox sparrows, and grackles are not found in western Washington state, where I live, but according to the Kiwibit app they are frequent visitors to my backyard. (I even had a “pileated woodpecker” visit the feeder, which would have been exceptionally rare, except the misidentified bird was a crow.) Also note that, unlike Birdfy feeders, the camera is not able to ID multiple birds on the feeder at a time. One area where Birdfy and Birdbuddy still beat their competitors is their intuitive, user-friendly apps. While Kiwibit’s non-subscription view has a simple interface, the subscription experience is a bit chaotic, as Kiwibit tries to cram a lot of information into too many places. There’s the tile view under “Birds,” the list of captures under “Feeds,” and a live view under “Live,” which you can click into to see a calendar of captures by day. Then, under “Me,” there’s a different calendar view with the number of bird visits per day, and a weekly Report tab that gives stats on that week’s visits. Even after four weeks of testing, I’m still not sure where I should first look when I simply want to see the birds that visited that day. Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro Rating: 7/10 The main reason for buying the Feeder 2 Pro is, of course, its dual-lens camera. If you have the subscription, clicking birds in the tile view will give you the option to download Ultra HD stills in different aspect ratios and with or without a watermark identifying the species, which is unique. Despite recording 4K footage at only 15 frames per second (fps), the camera’s bottom lens captured surprisingly crisp images of birds taking off, landing, and fighting. The camera’s top 1080p lens, meanwhile, offers 120 fps but only if you’re recording to an SD card. If you’re looking for a smart feeder that can produce quality stills and footage rivaling a budget action camera, the Feeder 2 Pro is what you want. The sensors don’t capture every bird visit, but unlike Birdbuddy, they only missed a handful here and there—not large swaths of the day. If needed, you can also record and save footage live through the app. The two solar panels built into the roof stayed fully charged throughout my testing, even on cloudy days. If something were to go wrong, there’s a removable 5,200-mAh battery in the bottom of the feeder that can be brought in to charge via USB-C. The Feeder 2's wonderfully designed, dual-compartment 1.7-liter seed hopper is on the Pro as well, with little stoppers that slide in and out to hold or release seed as needed. You can bring it into the house for filling without needing to take the whole feeder down. Upon unboxing, once the battery is charged, it takes just a few minutes to snap this IP65 (water-resistant against heavy rain) feeder together and pair it with the app. It runs on either 2.4- or 5.0-GHz Wi-Fi bands. Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro Rating: 7/10 Because so many features require an additional subscription, I’m not sure I would buy the Feeder 2 Pro as a gift, but I would consider buying it for myself. I don’t love that the full experience costs almost $100 extra per year, but it’s been fun to collect and share truly camera-quality images. Casual bird-watchers can find a more polished experience for less than half the price (see my recommendations here), but photography fans may find the image quality worth the app foibles and the recurring fee. Entrepreneurs are often told that success comes from taking risks. The advice sounds inspiring, but the best leaders rarely take blind risks. They make informed decisions with measured risk. Over the years, my brother Sterling and I have expanded healthcare companies, entered new markets, launched new service lines and managed through disruptions ranging from Hurricane Harvey to the pandemic. Along the way, I’ve learned that successful risk-taking is less about courage and more about structure. Every major decision carries uncertainty. The challenge is determining which risks deserve pursuit and which deserve patience. Whenever I face a significant decision — an expansion, a partnership, a new investment, a strategic pivot — I rely on a simple three-part framework to evaluate the opportunity and the downside before moving forward. Many entrepreneurs fall into one of two categories. The first group moves too quickly. They become excited by an opportunity and focus almost entirely on the upside. Revenue projections look promising, the market appears attractive, the idea feels exciting. The second group becomes trapped by analysis. They spend months gathering information, building projections and waiting for certainty before acting. Certainty rarely exists in business. But the alternative to waiting for it isn’t operating without knowledge. Effective leaders balance optimism with preparation: They pursue opportunities while planning for the setbacks that could occur along the way. That balance is the foundation of the framework below. The first question I ask is simple: What happens if this works? Too many business owners evaluate risk without fully defining the reward. Before considering obstacles, I want to understand the opportunity itself. Does this decision move the company closer to its long-term vision? Will it create meaningful growth or strengthen existing capabilities? When my brother and I evaluate expansion opportunities, we begin by asking whether the opportunity aligns with our broader mission. We are careful to avoid growth that creates complexity without advancing our long-term goals. A good opportunity should create leverage, not just more revenue. One exercise I recommend is writing down the three best outcomes that could result from a decision. It forces you to think strategically rather than emotionally. If the upside is limited, the risk may never be worth taking. The second part of the framework is about protection. I ask myself: What is the worst realistic outcome? Notice I said realistic. I evaluate what could reasonably go wrong and whether the organization can absorb the impact. During the pandemic, many business owners faced challenges they had never anticipated. Those with strong financial reserves, adaptable operations and contingency plans had far more options than those operating without safeguards. That experience reinforced one of my strongest business beliefs: Resilience is a competitive advantage. Before taking a major risk, I work through four questions: If the downside threatens the survival of the organization, I either restructure the opportunity or walk away. Protecting the downside keeps you in the game long enough to benefit from future opportunities. The final component is flexibility. I always ask: Can we adjust if conditions change? One lesson from periods of uncertainty is that adaptability often matters more than the original plan. During the pandemic, healthcare providers had to rethink how care was delivered. Those who adapted quickly recovered far faster than those waiting for conditions to return to normal. Whenever possible, I look for ways to reduce commitment while increasing learning. Can we test the concept before making a larger investment? Can we launch a pilot? Can we enter a market gradually instead of all at once? The ability to pivot creates options, and options reduce risk. One of the hardest leadership decisions is whether to keep pushing or change direction. Many entrepreneurs quit too early. Others stay committed long after the evidence suggests a different path. The key is separating temporary difficulty from structural problems. Temporary setbacks require persistence. Structural problems require adaptation. Persistence should always be tied to evidence: When data shows progress, continue. When evidence consistently points elsewhere, adapt. Failure carries value if you are willing to study it. Too many people view unsuccessful outcomes as personal defeats. I prefer to view them as feedback. Every setback contains information about assumptions, execution, timing or strategy. Some of our most valuable lessons came from situations that did not unfold as planned. Those experiences helped us build stronger systems, make better decisions and avoid bigger mistakes later. After every major decision, successful or not, I conduct a simple review: Leaders who consistently extract lessons from experience improve their decision-making over time. Before your next major decision, evaluate the opportunity, analyze the downside and assess your ability to adapt. That simple framework has guided Sterling and me through expansions, market disruptions, partnerships and the hardest leadership calls of our careers. A tailored version of OpenEvidence’s clinical search tool, running on Anthropic’s models, is rolling out across low- and middle-income countries. OpenEvidence, an AI tool used by American doctors, is now being offered in countries with limited access to medical literature. Reuters reported that the company is working with Anthropic to give clinicians in low- and middle-income countries free access to a specialized version of its platform. The initiative is being introduced in around 100 countries, including Uganda, Angola, Sudan, Haiti, and Mongolia, according to OpenEvidence, which provided the information to Reuters. The financial terms were not disclosed by either company. OpenEvidence answers doctors’ clinical questions using peer-reviewed research and treatment guidelines. It is currently free for clinicians in the United States and Europe. The companies say Anthropic provides the backend technology, while OpenEvidence adapts the system for each region’s healthcare needs. Founder Daniel Nadler told Reuters that US clinicians used the platform 42 million times in August. This year, OpenEvidence stated that it has been working with health organizations in Rwanda and Botswana to modify its tools for situations in which disease patterns. The resources available for diagnosis and the treatments on offer are very different from those found in richer countries; the project in Rwanda, carried out in partnership with the Rwanda Biomedical Center and Resolve to Save Lives, involved 45 local doctors and nurses who tested the tool and provided feedback on any necessary changes. “One hundred percent of what we are developing for these areas is designed to be context adaptive,” Nadler told Reuters. Critics of medical AI warn that systems trained mainly on data from high-income countries may not reflect how medicine is practiced elsewhere. In response, Nadler points out that even in places where clinics do not always have electricity, most doctors still have smartphones. Daniela Amodei, president of Anthropic, said the project is something the market could not achieve on its own. In her interview with Reuters, she explained that while the technology is now advanced enough, “market incentives by themselves would not cause it to happen” without some philanthropic effort. Also, we reported this week that Anthropic has built a laboratory for physical biology as it expands into drug science. For clinicians using the tool, the main issue is access, not AI itself. Dr Ahmed Bendary, a cardiologist at Benha University in Egypt, told Reuters that expanding the tool beyond the United States and Europe is especially important in places where access to major journals is limited. The key question now is whether a tool built mostly on evidence from wealthy countries can be adapted for use in places like Mongolia and Sudan, one country at a time. Contractors have been quietly handling some of the phone calls users ask the agent to make, according to internal posts.  If you ask Meta’s new AI agent to call a hairdresser’s salon, the person on the other end of the line might not be an AI. According to an exclusive report by Reuters on Tuesday, citing internal company postings, Meta has been testing a “human concierge” for Muse, with contractors taking over some of the calls placed through the agent. Last week Meta informed its staff about the trial, having previously launched the calling feature for Muse. For half of Meta’s employees, the ‘human agent calls’ option was enabled, with an opt-out for those who did not wish to participate. “Muse is now able to hand requests to a trained agent, who places the call and works it through,” the statement said, as reported by Reuters.  The posts indicated that some employees had warned that sensitive information could end up with the call-center contractors even though no one had intended it to happen. Daniel Roberts, a Meta spokesperson, told Reuters that employee feedback had been “overwhelmingly positive” and that the purpose of the test was to help shape the safety and privacy protections before its public release. He added that Meta would “only roll it out when it’s ready and with the proper disclosures”, although he didn’t specify what those disclosures would be or who would get them. Muse was launched in the United States on September 8 as an agent that sends out emails, makes purchases, and books travel on the user’s behalf. Its calling feature forwards requests to phone businesses so they can book a haircut, check stock, or obtain quotes, and then provides a transcript. The app has reached 2.5 million downloads, according to Sensor Tower data. At the time of its launch, Meta placed a strong emphasis on privacy, stating that each agent operates in its own virtual machine. While these statements refer to where the software runs, they say nothing regarding a person using a headset. The company has already been in this situation. Back in 2015, Facebook started testing M, a Messenger assistant supported by human ‘trainers’. It remained within a limited beta test and was closed down in 2018, since it had never achieved more than about 30% automation. Meta offers Muse as an agent who works on your behalf around the clock and has had assistance from someone on some calls. The stock has already fallen a shock-sized amount without a shock, which is what makes the next leg hard to size. Management attributes the increase to accelerated product development and go-to-market spending. That is the business sitting under a market value of about $6.5 billion. Hardly any of that price is paid for what D-Wave sells today. It is paid for what its quantum computers might sell later. Real customers, and a long wait. AT&T has expanded an agreement to apply D-Wave’s technology to optimization problems across its network operations, where one early application cut a process from about an hour to under 15 seconds. Florida Atlantic University bought a $20 million annealing quantum computer, part of $35.5 million in first-half bookings against $2.9 million a year earlier. It’s no secret that the economics of touring are tough for musicians, particularly independent artists. With such slim margins, artists have increasingly depended on merchandise to make up the difference. From T-shirts and totes to physical media sales, including vinyl and CDs, the merch booth can make touring viable and profitable for musicians both big and small.  	Beyond the physical merch booth, setting up an online storefront connects fans who can’t make it to the gig. For indie artists, getting started with online merch can be challenging, but there are online tools that can streamline the merch-selling process.   	Artist merch has gotten increasingly creative, expanding beyond T-shirts to housewares and quirky items inspired by lyrics and song titles. As for clothing, musicians are bridging the gap between merch and fashion.   	But not every artist can afford to hire an established designer or enlist a studio for their merch. Fortunately, something as simple as your album art on a blank tee can go a long way. By using the album art they already have for pieces like T-shirts, mugs, and sweatshirts, musicians can connect with fans and boost their revenue.       	One simple way to sell merch without needing to create new designs is DistroKid Direct. DistroKid, one of the leading online music distributors for independent musicians, has tools for musicians ranging from website creation to music mixing. Direct lets musicians upload their album art from their artist page to create pieces like T-shirts, sweatshirts, mugs, and tote bags.   	One of the challenges of selling merch is handling stock — between carrying the right shirt sizes and dealing with products that don’t sell, merch can carry its own logistical headaches. One option, particularly for artists who are still growing their fan base, is on-demand merch.   	Made-to-order merch can prevent unsold stock from piling up. While it’s not efficient for big artists selling a lot of T-shirts, it can be a great option for indie musicians who are just finding their footing.     DistroKid Direct utilizes this model, with pieces printed once the order is placed. That means artists don’t have to keep track of inventory or deal with storage. Artists can also set their own prices, and DistroKid only deducts the production cost. ActivisionBethesdaHaloNinja TheoryObsidianXbox  Yesterday, Xbox announced the next stage in its ongoing major restructuring, consolidating several studios and laying off another 268 as it works its way toward a planned total of around 3200 job cuts in the space of a year. Halo has been handed off to Activision as Halo Studios shrinks to support size, Rare and Age of Empires developer World’s Edge are also under the Activision banner now, Obsidian is moving under Bethesda, Turn 10 and Playground are merging, and Ninja Theory is entering consultation. Joost van Dreunen, NYU Stern professor and author of SuperJoost Playlist, is calling it “a reverse acquisition in slow motion.” “The publishers Xbox spent a fortune acquiring are now absorbing the studios Xbox built,” he wrote yesterday. I reached out to my usual cadre of analysts in the wake of this news to ask them what they make of this massive shake-up, and received back a series of emails full of deep concern, but little surprise. Both head of market analysis at Alinea Analytics Rhys Elliot and Omdia senior analyst James McWhirter brought up what they saw as Xbox’s identity crisis, with Elliott noting that Xbox has swapped roles to become a publisher first and a platform second, and McWhirter seeing it more as Xbox feeling pulled in both directions. “It still wants to be a console platform holder, yet its expanded remit as a multiplatform publisher has weakened its ability to compete with Sony and Nintendo on the same level,” McWhirter said. “Game Pass was meant to broaden the audience, but it instead diverted spend away from upfront purchases toward subscription revenue. “Put simply, its first-party portfolio hasn’t reached the potential Xbox would like it to because of its many conflicting objectives.” Even so, several of the analysts I spoke to saw some logic in some of the combinations, with both Elliott and Newzoo director of market intelligence Manu Rosier noting that a number of the smaller studios have been folded in with larger studios working in the same genre. “Activision leads shooters, Bethesda leads role-playing games, King leads casual, and Playground leads racing,” Rosier said. “One leadership per genre can plan releases across all its games. That can stop Microsoft titles from competing with each other for the same players and avoid gaps in the calendar. “Newzoo data shows why: since January 2025, players of Obsidian’s Avowed and The Outer Worlds 2 were more than three times more likely than average to also play Bethesda’s Starfield or The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered. Yet Avowed and The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Remastered launched just two months apart in 2025. Newzoo data shows PC and console playtime was flat in 2025. New games mostly take time away from existing ones. In a market this competitive, it makes sense to place fewer bets, each made by the most experienced team. “Ubisoft and Electronic Arts made similar moves. Ubisoft regrouped its studios into five genre-based Creative Houses in January 2026, and Electronic Arts brought four studios, including Criterion and Motive, under a single Battlefield Studios banner in 2025.” Like with the other shifts, some of the analysts see some silver linings to Activision taking on Halo. “The upshot of today’s announcement is that Activision is absorbing Xbox rather than the other way around,” van Dreunen said. “Halo, Rare, and World’s Edge now report to Rob Kostich, which means Microsoft’s most iconic franchise, its longest-held British studio, and its flagship RTS all sit inside the publisher it paid $69 billion for three years ago. Reducing Halo Studios to a support team ends a fifteen-year experiment in in-house stewardship and is a plain admission that it didn’t work, so the bet now is that the Call of Duty machine can do for Halo what it does every year for its own franchise.” Rosier seems to agree, and suggests that Halo and Call of Duty could “take turns.” “Shooters are more competitive than ever. Newzoo data shows their share of PC and console playtime fell from 39.6% to 34.8% in 2025, with both Fortnite and Call of Duty declining. That puts pressure on Call of Duty‘s annual release. Halo can relieve some of it because it reaches different players: since January 2025, fewer than 3% of Call of Duty players also played Halo Infinite. “Halo has never run on an annual cycle, and its last two mainline games launched six years apart. Now it sits under the leadership that ships Call of Duty every year. One possible scenario: Halo and Call of Duty alternate years, so Call of Duty no longer carries Microsoft’s shooter slot alone every year.” However, in Rosier’s opinion, Rare and World’s Edge feel like odd ones out. “Sea of Thieves and Age of Empires sit outside Activision’s shooter portfolio, and genre does not explain the move. It is the one part of the regrouping without a clear genre logic, which makes it the move to follow.” Elliott had even less optimism about this particular change. “Handing Halo to Activision and cutting Halo Studios down to a support team is essentially a demotion. Itâs wild, as Halo was the franchise that sold Xboxes. In our data the Campaign Evolved remake landed respectably but nowhere near what Halo used to mean. But part of that is because of the lack of online multiplayer. “Rare and World’s Edge is about publishing muscle, not creative fit. Sea of Thieves and Age of Empires have nothing in common with Call of Duty except they now sit under the group Xbox trusts to operate at scale.” Everyone I spoke to had less to say about Ninja Theory, likely due to the obscurity around what had actually happened with the two deals for the studio that fell through. Rosier posited that “investors may be wary of single-player games with a niche audience.” And van Dreunen put it this way: “The Ninja Theory situation is the most troubling item. When two sale agreements collapse for the studio behind Hellblade, it tells you the 2018 acquisition spree bought talent that turns out to be hard to sell and expensive to keep. It’s a costly lesson and one I hope Xbox and its peers will remember during the next cycle. As I’ve mentioned previously, Asha Sharma is working to make Xbox smaller. She is reducing the number of studios, removing management layers, and delegating responsibility for franchises to whichever label has a record of shipping on schedule.” I did speak to one other analyst on this subject overall: Dr. Serkan Toto of Kantan Games. He was unsurprised when I emailed him. “I already predicted earlier this year Asha will run through the Xbox business like a bulldozer, and sadly, this has now become reality.” Toto brought up several major concerns he has about the move overall. He’s worried that studios “might lose their identity and soul” by merging with others, such as Halo with Activision or Obsidian with Bethesda. And he’s worried this reorganization will better enable Sharma to sell off studios or disband them if things don’t go well…which, they very well may not. “Success is not guaranteed,” he said. “If this restructuring does not work, we might look at even more pain in the years going forward.” “One thing is clearer than ever: Project Helix must absolutely hit,” he concludes. If you weren’t already aware, it will probably come as no surprise to hear that the pioneering computer-animation studio Pixar built its early workflow on Silicon Graphics SGI workstations. These were beefy Unix machines that, as the name implied, were developed for graphical work. When the age of the RISC workstation came to a close, many Unix users were pushed onto Windows NT — but not at Pixar. At Pixar, they learned to love the penguin. It comes down to hardware rather than software. You know the story: PCs got faster and cheaper with different vendors competing for a giant market, while the world of RISC workstations couldn’t keep its lead. Pixar would have been happy staying on Unix workstations, even SGIs if that had been a practical option — but with every project increasing the load on the render farms, it wasn’t. Yet Pixar’s entire workflow was predicated on a Unix environment. They had written a couple million lines of code for their internal use, and really didn’t want to port it over to Windows, even after a mistaken rm command nearly cost the world Toy Story 2. Adam Stewart, executive chairman of Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts, asserted that the deal enables faster growth with a partner sharing their values. A 10x forward EBITDA multiple on a marquee all-inclusive brand isn’t obviously stretched for a business with proven pricing power, according to Royal Caribbean. A debt-funded move into land-based resorts is a different operating model from running ships, and the market prices execution and leverage well before any earnings contribution shows up. Reporter 2 Reporter 2 September 23, 2026, 9:00 am ET This news is not for people who like to lie on their resume. LinkedIn is adding new ways to verify where you work and went to school, the company announced on Wednesday. The new verifications for members and companies come amid a torrent of AI-powered scams wreaking havoc on social media platforms and the job market. Generative AI makes it easier to create fake media or impersonate specific people, like recruiters or executives. “With advancements in AI, pretending to be someone that you’re not is getting increasingly cheaper and easier,” Oscar Rodriguez, vice president of LinkedIn’s trust products, told me in an interview. “And with that, authenticity is becoming increasingly important, perhaps more important than it has ever been.” As of September, more than 115 million of LinkedIn’s billion members have added verifications to their profiles.  Individual LinkedIn members can verify their current workplace or university by getting two or more colleagues to vouch for them. You’ll need to have been connected to the person vouching for you for at least one year and have two-factor authentication enabled. You won’t be able to vouch for every single person you went to school with or in your office, but those limits are designed to ensure bad actors don’t take advantage of the tool. Requests to verify your classmates and colleagues will appear under a new, separate section under My Network. LinkedIn says verified accounts see 50% more engagement on their posts and nearly 90% more profile views.  And if you’re a page admin for a company page on LinkedIn, you can now also remove people falsely claiming to work at your company from LinkedIn’s search results. This is less about cutting down on clout chasers than it is about weeding out scammers who may falsely claim to be a recruiter or executive with a company in order to glean money and personal information from job hunters. Job scams are a growing problem; in a March 2026 survey from the cybersecurity firm Norton, 33% of US respondents said they had encountered a fake recruiter, phishing attempt or fraudulent job posting. Those who fell victim almost always lost money, nearly $9,000 each on average. Verification on LinkedIn is free, but it’s a little bit different than other social media platforms. In addition to claiming a person is who they say they are, these tools can also verify where someone goes to school and works.  Once you do verify these things, people who view your LinkedIn profile will be prompted to view your verifications when their mouse hovers over your name. You’ll also get an icon that looks like a checkmark inside a shield next to your name. This is the badge you want to look for on company pages when you see a new job listing and get a message from someone claiming to be a recruiter.
